# Imagery Pictures are where generated pages most obviously give up: a grey box, an icon in a square, a fake dashboard, an abstract blob. This file is how to decide what the pictures are, where to find real ones, how to crop and place them, and what to do when there are none. ## Contents 1. What the study measured 2. Decide what imagery exists 3. Real pictures from the open collections 4. The dealt photographs 5. Cropping and placing 6. Treatment 7. Showing software 8. Drawing the subject 9. Type and colour alone 10. Markup and credits 11. Video 12. Where pictures and footage go ## 1. What the study measured - On 60% of the studied sites one piece of media covers at least half of the first screen; on half of them it covers nearly all of it. Top-scored sites: 68% and 56%. Weak sites: 48% and 39%. - Only 15% of heroes have no media at all, and those are deliberate typographic statements. - Media has square corners on 73% of sites. Where corners are rounded the usual radius is about 12px, applied to every image alike. - Top-scored pages carry far more imagery (a median of 37 images against 5 on weak pages): the strong sites show, the weak ones tell. - What the imagery is, by the panel's classification: a mix of kinds 32%, photography 14%, generative or WebGL scenes 13%, real product interface 12%, 3D renders 11%, illustration 9%, video 6%, type only 3%. - Among the 54 sites the panel scored under 6.8, legibility (text lost over a busy image, or too little contrast) was named as a weakness in 13. - In the October 2026 study of 91 Awwwards Sites of the Day (section 12), the median page carries 7 pictures (top sites 8, the lowest 2) and footage appears on 42% of sites (half of the top ones, one of the 16 lowest). - Pictures come in whole screens: 42% of scrolled screens hold none and 19% are 90% picture or more. - 94% of pictures have square corners, and on a typical site two ratios hold three-quarters of them. ## 2. Decide what imagery exists In order of preference: 1. **The project's own images.** Product shots, the place, the people, the work. Even ordinary photographs of the real thing beat beautiful photographs of something else. Ask what exists; look in the repository. 2. **Images you can generate** with an image tool in this session. Write prompts as a photographer's brief: subject, angle, light, background, crop ratio, and "no text". Generate the hero first and make the rest match its light. 3. **Real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections** (section 3). Archives, museums and photographers have published millions of pictures anyone may use with a credit: the client's city and street in old postcards, maps of its neighbourhood, its materials, its trade in engravings, museum objects of its kind. Whenever an honest one exists, it beats a drawing of the same thing: it is real, it has detail no drawing in a page's budget reaches, and it carries history. Honest means nobody could take it for the client's own product, room, dish, person or team. 4. **Pictures you draw in code from the subject itself** (section 8), for what no honest picture exists of: the product's own objects as flat shapes, the place's tiles and windows, a map of its streets, the document a tool produces, the interface of a piece of software. In testing, pages that drew their subject with care beat pages that borrowed unrelated photographs every time, and beat pages that showed nothing. 5. **The photographs dealt on the direction sheet.** Real photographs of places, light, texture and weather. Use them only where an honestly generic picture fits (the open sea for a house on the sea, fog for a quiet retreat). They cannot stand in for a specific product, dish, room, person or screen: a foggy motorway on a restaurant page reads as stock at once, and jurors notice. 6. **Type and colour alone,** done on purpose (section 9). Tell `draw.mjs` the truth with `--have`. If you have no product photographs and no image tool, do not pass `product-photo`; the draw will avoid the directions that depend on showing the object. Pictures found in the open collections are not the project's own: do not pass `photography` for them. ## 3. Real pictures from the open collections `scripts/assets.mjs` searches four open sources without keys and prints, for each find, a direct image URL, the page it comes from, its size, its creator, its licence and a credit line: - **Openverse**: one index over Flickr, Wikimedia Commons, museums and libraries. - **Wikimedia Commons**: archival photographs, old maps, scans of prints and books, places as they look now. - **The Art Institute of Chicago** and **The Metropolitan Museum of Art**: public-domain paintings, prints, drawings, photographs, textiles and objects, in large scans. ```bash node /scripts/assets.mjs "ghent postcard" node /scripts/assets.mjs "fig" --source museums --orientation portrait node /scripts/assets.mjs "basalt texture" --min-width 2400 --source openverse,commons node /scripts/assets.mjs --get commons:36649959,met:707892 # download, record the credits node /scripts/assets.mjs --credits # footer line and report list ``` By default it keeps only licences that allow commercial use (CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA) and pictures at least 1000 pixels wide, and checks that every image it prints actually loads. `--license pd` keeps only pictures that need no credit; `--orientation`, `--min-width` and `--limit` narrow the list; `--source` picks the sources; `--json` gives the raw results. Each result has a ref (`commons:36649959`) that `--get` takes. **What to search for.** The inventory (SKILL.md step 1), not the category: "bakery" finds other people's bakeries. The subject's world is specific: - **Its place:** the city, the street, the harbour, the valley, in old postcards and photographs ("ghent postcard", "rotterdam harbour 1920") and as it looks today ("gent korenmarkt"). - **Its maps:** the street plan, the chart of its bay, the geology of its valley ("ghent old map", "nautical chart lisbon"). - **Its materials,** close enough to read as a surface: the stone of its quay, the grain of its oak, its glaze, its tiles ("azulejo tiles", "basalt cobblestones", "oak grain"). - **Its trade's history:** the old tools, the craft in engravings and trade catalogues, patent drawings ("bread oven engraving", "potter's wheel", "bicycle patent drawing"). - **Museum objects of its kind,** with `--source museums`: a coffee set from about 1810 for a studio that makes coffee sets, a woodblock print of a wave for a surf school, a porcelain plate painted with figs for a fig orchard. - **Scientific imagery:** botanical and zoological plates ("botanical engraving fig"), star charts, microscope photographs, satellite views of its coast, geological sections. Search in the place's own words (azulejo, not "blue tile"; Korenmarkt, not "market square"), add a medium (postcard, engraving, old map, lithograph, aerial photograph) or a decade, and try two or three queries per idea. The museum sources match best on one or two words ("fig", "harbour", "teapot"). **What makes a good find.** - It belongs to this subject's world and would not fit the nearest competitor's page. - It still reads at the crop the slot needs. Look at it before deciding: `--get` downloads it, then open the file. A title is not a picture. - It is large enough: twice the width it is shown at for anything full-bleed (the script prints the largest size available). A 1024-pixel Flickr photograph is a half-width picture at most. - It belongs to one family with the others on the page: all engravings, or all photographs from one era, or all close surfaces in one light. A 1900 postcard beside a modern stock photograph beside a botanical plate reads as a scrapbook. - No watermark, no burned-in text or logo, no frame or scanner edge you cannot crop away, and no recognisable living person who could be taken for the client's staff or customers. **Use it creatively.** Found pictures are material, not decoration: - **One archival photograph as the hero,** full-bleed: the street as it was a century ago, behind the name of the business that stands in it today, with the year in the caption. - **A museum engraving enlarged until its line becomes texture,** cropped tight and returning at different scales as the page's one motif (the whole fig plate in the hero, a single leaf of it beside the menu). - **An engraving or a map on white paper set with `mix-blend-mode: multiply` on the page's colour field,** so the ink sits on the ground (section 6). - **The real map of the street as the contact section,** the door marked, the north and the scale taken from the original. - **A material close-up as a whole field:** the quay's stone behind the opening hours. - **A run of old postcards or plates as the gallery,** one size, one treatment. Treatments stay within section 6: untouched, greyscale for the whole set, or multiply on a field. **Stay honest.** - **A found picture is never the client's own.** It may show the client's city, its materials, its history, the kind of thing it makes; it may never stand in for the client's product, room, dish, person, team or customers. If a visitor could take it for the client's own (a bakery counter, a plate of pasta, a smiling barista, a guest room), do not use it. - **Caption from the source** when a caption helps: what it is and when, as the archive describes it ("Gand, unloading a steamer, 1905"). Never write a caption that ties it to the client. - **Record and credit every picture.** `--get` writes the source, creator, licence and page of each download to `assets/credits.json`. CC BY and CC BY-SA require a credit with the title, the creator, a link to the source and a link to the licence; `--credits` prints them as one line of HTML for the footer (section 10). Public-domain pictures need no credit; give one anyway. - **Respect the licence.** CC BY-SA: an altered version (recoloured, combined with other pictures) must be shared under the same licence. Non-commercial (NC) and no-derivatives (ND) licences are out for a client's site, which is why the script leaves them out unless asked. Read the `note` lines: some pictures carry personality rights or a trademark, are public domain only in the United States, or come with an archive's statement instead of a licence. - **Download, do not hotlink.** Save what you use into the project: `--get` puts it in `assets/` at 1920 pixels wide (pass `--width 1280` for a picture shown at half the screen, `--width 3840` for a very large hero where the source has it). The page then works offline, does not break when an archive moves a file, and does not load from someone else's server. Every licence the script allows by default permits copying. - **List them in the report:** file, title, creator, licence, source page, and where the credit sits. `--credits` prints that list too. If two or three honest queries per idea find nothing that fits, draw (section 8). A drawing made for the subject is better than a found picture that is merely nearby. If the script cannot reach any source (no network), draw, and say so in the report. For moving pictures, the same script searches real footage with `--video` (section 11). ## 4. The dealt photographs - The sheet lists eight from one set so they share a subject and a light. Use three to six. - Each line says where the calm area is. Put text there or keep text off the image. - More from the same or another set: `node scripts/draw.mjs --photos list`, `--photos `, or `--photos "fog coast"` to search descriptions. - URLs have the form `https://picsum.photos/id///`. Request the exact pixel size you render at twice the CSS size for sharpness, capped around 2400 wide. Add `?grayscale` for black-and-white. - These are photographs from Unsplash served by Lorem Picsum under the Unsplash licence. List the ids you used in your report; they are meant to be replaced by the project's own pictures. ## 5. Cropping and placing - **Choose a small set of ratios and stick to them:** for example 4:5 for portraits, 16:10 for landscapes and 1:1 for details. Random ratios look like a stock dump. - **Go large.** A photograph at full width, or at half the screen and full height, has presence. Six small ones in a grid have none. If the image is good, give it the room; if it is not, cut it. - **Crop with intent.** Use `object-fit: cover` with an `object-position` chosen per image so the subject sits where the composition needs it (off-centre, on a third, against the text side). - **Let images touch edges.** Full-bleed, or bleeding off one side, reads as designed. An image floating with equal margins on all sides reads as placed by default. - **Overlap sparingly and on purpose:** a headline whose last line runs over the top edge of the picture, a small image overlapping a large one by a fixed 40–80px. One overlap per screen at most. - **Square corners** unless the direction or the one-motif shape says otherwise. If rounded, one radius for every image on the page. - **No frames:** no borders, no shadows, no device mock-ups, no browser chrome around pictures. - **Captions** are one short line in the small size and soft ink under the image, left-aligned to its edge. Most images need none. - Where each picture goes on the page, how large, and what the phone does with it: section 12. ## 6. Treatment One treatment for the whole page: - **Untouched.** The default. Pick images whose light already agrees. - **Greyscale.** `filter: grayscale(1) contrast(1.05)`, or `?grayscale` on the URL. Unifies a mixed set instantly and suits editorial and typographic directions. Apply to every image or none. - **Multiply on a field.** On a light flat ground, `mix-blend-mode: multiply` makes a white studio background vanish so a product sits directly on the colour. - **Darkened for a dark page.** `filter: brightness(0.85) contrast(1.05)` so the image edges sink into the ground. Not treatments: colour washes over photographs, duotone overlays, blur, grain overlays, vignettes, tilted "polaroid" frames with shadows. For text on a photograph, a neutral scrim covering only the text area: a solid block at 40–55% black, or a fade from 55% black to transparent over the lower third. Never a coloured overlay. ## 7. Showing software - Build a real fragment of the interface in HTML at its true size, with believable content, instead of a shrunken screenshot or a decorative mock-up. Crop to the part that makes the point: one control, one row, one panel. - Believable means real labels, real numbers that add up, one item hovered or selected, proper alignment. Grey bars standing in for text are worse than no image. - Put the fragment directly on the page or on one flat stage colour. No laptop, no phone frame unless the product is a phone app and the frame is a plain rounded rectangle. - Inside a fragment the product's own interface conventions apply (its small radii, its 1px control borders, a shadow on its open menu). Put the attribute `data-ui` on the fragment's root element: the inspector and the linter then leave what is inside alone, and hold the page around it to the house rules. `data-ui` is for cropped fragments only; wrapping a heading or a whole section in it fails. Write the fragment's CSS under a `[data-ui]` selector (`[data-ui] .row { … }`) so the linter can tell it apart from page styles. - If the user supplies real screenshots, show them large and uncropped at least once. ## 8. Drawing the subject When nothing real can be photographed and the open collections hold no honest picture of it, draw it, and draw it well. Inline SVG and CSS are enough. Drawings and found pictures can share a page: the found ones show the world around the client, the drawings show the client's own things. - **Draw the subject's own things,** not decoration: the stool's three legs and the grain of its seat, the enamel sign over the bakery door, the hut's two windows and its stove pipe, the street plan, the invoice the tool produces, the festival's stage. If you cannot name what a drawing depicts in the subject's world, it is decoration. - **One graphic language for the whole page:** flat filled shapes, no outlines or one consistent stroke weight, the same corner and curve vocabulary everywhere, drawn in the palette's real colours (fields and accent at full strength, not greys). A set of drawings that obviously belong together reads as an identity; a mix of styles reads as clip art. - **Colour is the material.** A product sold on its finish is drawn in that finish's colours; a sea house in the sea's blues and the sand; never a page of grey placeholders. - **Draw with three levels of detail.** Jurors called simple drawings "basic" every time. Give each drawing big shapes that read at a glance, middle shapes that describe the thing (the handle, the window frame, the step), and small details that reward a second look (the maker's mark, the house number, the chipped tile, the hinge, a bird on the roof). Make light with flat tone steps (a lit face and a shaded face of each volume), not gradients. A drawing that would pass as a placeholder icon at full size is not finished. - **Draw large and let it work:** the drawing is the hero's dominant element, a full-width band, a set of tiles, the footer mark. Small doodles scattered around read as filler. - **Let it carry the idea through the page,** the way a motif does: the same drawn object returns at different scales, the tile grid becomes the opening hours, the map becomes the booking section. - **Honesty:** say plainly, in small text near the first drawing or in the footer, that the pictures are drawn until photographs exist, if the client might otherwise be taken to be showing real products. In your report, list which drawings are placeholders for photography. - **Not this:** gradient-shaded 3D-looking blobs, isometric clip art, generic line illustrations of people at laptops, abstract floating shapes, icons in squares. Those are the generated look. ## 9. Type and colour alone This is a legitimate design, not a gap to disguise. Only 7 of the studied sites use no imagery at all, and they hold their own: a median panel score of 7.5 against 7.2 for the whole set. - Make the typography the image: one statement at 10–14vw, a list set at 5vw, numerals at display size. - Use colour at scale: a full field, an inverted section, a two-field split. - Use the subject's own shape as one flat motif if the direction calls for it (a circle, an arc, a notch), drawn in CSS, cropped by the viewport. - Do not add: icons in squares, abstract gradients, dot grids, wave dividers, floating shapes, emoji, generic line illustrations, or an empty box where a picture "will go". ## 10. Markup and credits A found picture, downloaded into the project with `--get`, used as the hero: ```html ``` A dealt photograph further down the page: ```html ``` The credits, as `--credits` prints them, in the footer: ```html

Pictures: “Fig (Ficus carica L.): 57 segments of flowers and fruits”, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

``` - Always `width` and `height` (or `aspect-ratio` in CSS) so nothing jumps while loading. - `loading="lazy"` on everything except the hero image, which gets `fetchpriority="high"`. - `alt` describes the picture in plain words. Decorative repeats get `alt=""`. The script's suggested alt is the archive's title; rewrite it to say what the picture shows. - A coloured `background-color` on the image container (the ground or surface tone) so the layout is whole before the image arrives. - The credit line is part of the footer's design, at full contrast, with its links. Set it at the body size; one step smaller only on a page with plenty of running text, because a long credit line in small type can become the page's most common text size and fail the inspector's body-size check. One line for all pictures; no credit captions laid over the pictures themselves. Credit only the pictures the page still uses. - A broken image fails the inspector. Check every picture in the screenshots. ## 11. Video A moving picture of the subject's world can carry a section the way a photograph does: the river at the end of the street, the roaster's drum turning, a timber frame going up. `assets.mjs --video` searches real footage without keys: Wikimedia Commons (every video there comes with web-sized transcodes; the best source for short clips), the Internet Archive's Prelinger Archives (industrial, educational, city and home films from the 1920s to the 1970s, mostly public domain and mostly long) and NASA (the Earth from orbit, launches, aircraft, laboratories). The rest of the Internet Archive is left out: anyone can upload there, and the licence claims are unchecked. ```bash node /scripts/assets.mjs "coffee roasting" --video node /scripts/assets.mjs "river" --video --source commons,nasa --orientation landscape node /scripts/assets.mjs --get commons:49769620 # the clip, a poster frame, the credit ``` It takes a rendition of 720p or smaller (`--res` changes that), lists short clips first, prints each clip's length and file size, and flags anything over 25 MB or longer than a minute. `--get` refuses a clip over 25 MB unless you pass `--max-mb`, and saves the source's still frame beside it as the poster (Commons and NASA; the archive's own stills are too small). An archive film of ten minutes is too heavy as it stands: trim a few seconds from it with ffmpeg if it is installed, or choose a shorter clip. Licences, credits and honesty work exactly as for pictures (section 3). **Choosing a clip.** - **Short:** 5 to 20 seconds that loop without a visible jump: water, smoke, a turning drum, traffic, leaves, a crowd from far away. Watch it to the end before choosing. - **Light:** under about 5 MB for a section and 10 MB for a hero. In the study sources are 1920×1080 (the commonest) or 1280×720, median length 10 s; 720p is plenty behind type. For a full-bleed hero, cut a tall 720×1280 version for the phone, or set `object-position` on the subject. - **Clean:** no slate, title card, logo, watermark or burned-in caption. NASA and archive films often open with a slate, and the source's poster frame may be that slate. No recognisable person who could be taken for the client's staff or customers. - **Never the client's own:** a found clip of a roastery is not this roastery. - **Found clips: one per page, two at most.** A found clip shows the world around the client; a third makes a theme of it. The project's own footage can carry more: in the study a site with footage carries a median of three or four clips. Either way, **one moving picture per screen**; two loops running side by side are noise. **On the page.** - Muted, looping, inline, with a poster and a fixed size, as `--get` prints it: ``. No sound and no controls on a decorative loop. `aria-hidden` because it is decoration: whatever the clip says that matters belongs in the text beside it. - The poster shows before the clip plays, on slow connections and under reduced motion, so it must work as a picture on its own. If the source's still is a slate or a blur, take a frame from the clip yourself or use a found picture. - In the study only 31% of clips had a poster, and the panel recorded the blank and grey boxes before they played as faults. Here every clip has one. - Play a clip only while it is in view, and none under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, where the poster shows instead: ```html ``` - Crop and place it like a photograph (sections 5 and 6): `object-fit: cover`, one ratio, square corners, no frame, a ground-coloured `background-color` while it loads. - Never under body text. On a clip put a headline, one line and one action at most, and check the contrast where they sit across the whole loop, not only on the poster: footage that is dark at one second can be bright at the next. If any frame drops below 4.5:1 (3:1 for 24px and up), use the scrim in section 6 or move the text off the clip. Nothing lies on top of a headline or a statement. - It is motion: let it be the page's one moving thing, or sit in a section where nothing else moves. - Credit it with the pictures: `--credits` prints one footer line for both ("Pictures and footage:") and the list for the report, with each clip's length. - Where footage goes (hero background, inline loop, the frame that grows, a docked card), and what the study measured about it: section 12. Nothing that matters plays on hover only, and a full film with sound sits behind a play button that opens a player with controls. ## 12. Where pictures and footage go What strong pages do with their pictures, measured on the latest 100 Awwwards Sites of the Day (10 July to 17 October 2026, captured at 1440×900 and 390×844). 91 were usable. A panel described where every picture sat and scored each site the Awwwards way, and a script measured how much of each screen is picture. "Top" means a panel score of 7.5 or more (36 sites), "lowest" under 7.3 (16 sites). The scores sit close together (6.7 to 7.9) and a single score carries about half a point of noise, so read the links between a placement and the score as leanings, not laws. ### How much of each screen is picture - **All or nothing.** Counting photographs, footage and picture backgrounds (not canvases), the median scrolled screen in the study is 16% picture, but few screens sit near it: 42% hold no picture and 19% are 90% picture or more. Only 19% fall between 20% and 60%. A picture either leads its screen or stays out of it. - **About a third, with rests.** On the 67 sites that put pictures in the page, the average screen is 36% picture (middle half 18–69%). Top sites sit at 30% and leave 28% of their screens with no picture at all: screens of type are the rests between picture screens. - **The first screen.** A picture covers at least half of it on 41% of the sites and nearly all of it on 32%. A full-bleed photograph or film is the whole first screen on 29%; footage is the main hero picture on about a quarter. - **A scene is not a picture.** 66 of the 91 keep a WebGL canvas over at least 30% of the screen, so counting canvases the median screen is entirely covered. On the lowest-scored sites that canvas is often all there is: the five lowest usable sites (6.7 to 7.0) draw everything in it and put two pictures at most in the page. - **Text is small in area.** The median screen is 8% text. Type is set large and sparse around the pictures, not packed beside them. - **Off-centre.** Measured per section across the crawled sites, pictures sit to the left or right 939 times, centred 273 times, and full-bleed or behind text 269 times. - **The phone carries more picture,** not less: 19% of a phone screen at the median, and 27% of the first phone screen against 17% on desktop. Full-bleed pictures re-crop to portrait and fill the screen; splits put the picture first at full width. ### How many - **Seven pictures per page** at the median (middle half 1–25). Top sites 8 (middle half 4–27), lowest 2 (0–4). The floor in SKILL.md step 6, four and usually six to twelve, is the strong half of the study. - **Footage on 42% of sites:** on half of the top sites and half of the middle band, and on one of the 16 lowest. A site with footage carries a median of three or four clips. - **Three to five placements.** Sites that use two or fewer of the placements below average 7.31; sites that use three or more average about 7.5. The median top site uses four, the median lowest site one. The commonest way strong pages pair words and a picture. - *Geometry.* The picture takes 42% of the width at the median (middle half 33–49%), up to two-thirds, at the full height of its section: 680×850 and 720×900 are typical. 38% of these pictures are portrait, mostly 4:5 or 3:4. The text starts on the 50% line (x = 720) or on the line where the picture ends, top-aligned or docked low, not centred in its half. Let the picture touch the viewport on its outer side: only about 30% do in the study, and the ones with margin on every side read as placed by default (section 5). Alternate sides only across three or more rows. - *Phone.* Picture first at full width (4:5, or 4:3 for a landscape), text under it. - *Fails.* The same split in three sections running; a picture floating in the middle of its half; a text column narrower than about 30 characters. **Full-bleed band** - *When.* One picture carries a whole screen between type screens: the place, the work, the object at full size. The picture holds one half (685×880 is a typical portrait), two-thirds, or the whole screen with the text passing over it on a solid panel. Text rows about 150px apart, so two or three are in view at once. - *Phone.* Release the stick: picture first, text under it. If the picture swaps per item, keep it as a band in the top 40% of the screen. - *Fails.* Long runways where the text has faded out and the held picture is all that is left (the panel recorded several empty stages on phones); body copy set on the held picture. **Inset frame that grows** - *When.* Once per page, for the film or picture the page is about, as the move from type into picture. - *Geometry.* The frame starts centred at 35–50% of the width (549×366, 710×480 and 864×540 in the study) or as a 16px inset round a full screen, and grows to the full width and height over 720–2,700px of scroll. Any corner radius goes to 0 as it reaches the edges. A headline sits above it before it starts; nothing else on the screen moves while it grows. - *Phone.* Start at full width inside the 16px margins and grow to a full-bleed portrait, or skip the growth. - *Fails.* The growth is the only thing on screen for three scrolls; a loading spinner or a blank box in the first frame (give it a poster, start loading before it enters); used twice. **Uneven mosaic** - *When.* A body of work, or one place seen several ways: five to twelve pictures. - *Geometry.* Two columns, or rows of three on a 24-column grid. Two or three picture widths (for example 32%, 48% and 65% of the width, or 5, 7 and 12 columns), neighbours offset vertically by 120–190px, 130–450px between rows, one or two ratios, a caption under each. - *Phone.* One column alternating full width and about 70% width, or two columns of 120–180px tiles that keep the offsets. - *Fails.* Random ratios with random offsets, which read as a stock dump. Captions in 9–12px mono with index numbers, the award-site habit: here the caption is one line in the text face at body size, with no number. **Horizontal gallery** - *When.* A set people browse in any order: products, rooms, events, a team. - *Geometry.* Cards 25–35% of the width (435×326 with 20px gaps at 1440: three in full and a fourth cut by the edge), or a strip at one fixed height with mixed widths (576px tall in the study), or a slider whose centre slide is about 73% of the width with 170–180px of each neighbour showing. Always cut by the right edge so it reads as more. A marquee of pictures moves slowly: 60–120s per loop. - *Phone.* One card at 75–80% of the width (290–300px of 390) with the next one showing; swipe. - *Fails.* Arrows and no drag or swipe; a marquee of things people need to read; a carousel holding the page's one important picture. **Panel sliding over a held picture** - *When.* A change of chapter: the picture holds, and the next section rises over it. - *Geometry.* The picture is sticky at 100vh; the next section's ground slides up over it at full width, its top edge straight or shaped from the subject (the study has the arch of a building's windows). Here it is a solid panel with square corners: no rounded sheet tops, no frosted glass. - *Phone.* Unchanged. - *Fails.* Decks of five or six cards whose earlier cards linger as slivers; stacking for its own sake. **Even grid** - *When.* An archive only (layout.md §5): a shop range, the team, a menu, the full list of work. - *Geometry.* Two, three or four across, equal cells, 8–16px gaps, one ratio (4:5 is the commonest), the caption under each picture. - *Phone.* Two across for products, one for work and people. - *Fails.* Three equal cards as "features". Cards with a dark gradient at the foot so the label can sit on the picture, common in the study: here the label goes under the picture. **Index with hover preview** - *When.* A list of eight or more projects or clients where the names matter as much as the pictures. - *Geometry.* Rows on a 45–80px pitch, names at 30–60px. One picture at a time, about a third of the width at 16:9 or a portrait 300–450px tall, at a fixed place (the right half from the 50% line, or the centre), swapped within 0.3s. A version that needs no mouse: the names scroll across a picture fixed at the centre and the picture shows whichever name is crossing it. In the study the picture sits on top of the names; here nothing lies on top of large type, so the names pass in front of it. - *Phone.* No hover. Give each row a thumbnail about 100px wide, or use the scroll version. - *Fails.* Pictures that never appear on a touch screen. Rows divided by hairlines, the award-site habit: here rows are separated by space, and the active row by ink or a change of ground. **One picture on a field, or one small picture beside a statement** - *When.* A pause in the page: a single portrait or object. Or a small picture that gives a statement a face. - *Geometry.* A single centred picture at 3:4 and 75% of the viewport height, on a ground taken from the picture. Or a small picture 7–26% of the width (108–374px) beside, above or between the lines of a 48–136px statement, aligned to one of its lines. - *Phone.* The picture above the statement at 60–100% of the width. - *Fails.* Used as the default for every picture: a picture with equal margins on all sides reads as placed by default (section 5). **Small pictures between words** - *When.* A statement about the things themselves (materials, people, products), on a screen of its own. - *Geometry.* Two to four chips in the statement, from the cap height to three-quarters of the type size tall and one to one and a half times as wide (50×46px in a 60px line; 113×75px between the two words of a 150px name), all from one shoot, square corners. Give them a width and height so the lines do not jump while they load. - *Phone.* Keep them inline at the height of the text. - *Fails.* More than four; chips from different shoots; a chip that carries information the words do not. **Picture inside or behind display type** - *When.* The object is the subject: a product, a building, a person. - *Geometry.* A small picture window sits inside a block of 150–200px display type and later opens into the next screen; or the object stands behind the type, showing between and around the letters; or it touches the edge of the word without covering a letter. In the study the object more often stands in front and covers one or two letters, or a line of type runs behind a square picture; here nothing lies on top of a headline (the inspector fails large text a fifth or more hidden), so the type stays in front. - *Phone.* Keep it, with the type at about 15vw, and check the word still reads. - *Fails.* An object over the letters; type displaced or glitched by the picture. **Cut-out object on a flat field** - *When.* Products and objects. The highest mean score in the table, on 7 of the 36 top sites. - *Geometry.* The object at 35–60% of the width on a flat ground taken from its own colours, standing on the bottom edge or running off one side, with the type behind or beside it. - *Phone.* The object at 80–90% of the width under the headline. - *Fails.* A render floating in a void with no ground; a drop shadow added to a cut-out (no resting shadows here; keep a contact shadow only if it was photographed). **Scattered collage** - *When.* Archives, ephemera, a festival of many small things. Sparingly: it is about as common on the lowest pages as on the top ones. - *Geometry.* Six to sixteen pictures of 100–300px at a few sizes around a centred heading, never over it. - *Phone.* Re-stack as overlapping pairs in one column. - *Fails.* Tilted prints and stickers with offset shadows, common in the study and not a treatment here (section 6); pictures crossing the text. **Small card docked in a corner** - *When.* A standing pointer to the reel or to the next thing. - *Geometry.* About 216×144 to 240×140, 30–43px from the corner; one per page. - *Phone.* Drop it, or move it into the flow. - *Fails.* Content scrolling under it; a second one. **3D gallery** - *What.* Pictures on a ring, sphere, helix or tunnel in a WebGL scene, turned by the wheel or by dragging. - *In the study.* 12 sites, 4 of them among the 16 lowest; mean score 7.30 against 7.44, usability 5.9 against 6.35. - *Here.* Do not build one. Show the same pictures as an index with previews or a horizontal gallery. ### Footage **What the study measured.** - Footage on 38 of 91 sites (42%): 18 of the 36 top sites, 19 of the 39 in the middle, 1 of the 16 lowest. A site with footage carries a median of three or four clips (middle half 1–8). - Footage covers at least half of the first screen on about a quarter of the sites, and is full-bleed on nearly all of them. - Clips are short: median 10s, middle half 5–14s; 61% run 10s or less and 88% 20s or less. - Every decorative clip is muted, loops, plays inline and has no controls. The autoplay attribute is on 44% of clips; the rest are started by script, mostly as they come into view. - Only 31% of clips have a poster (13 of the 38 sites). The rest show a blank or grey box until they play, and the panel recorded those as blank first paints. Here a poster is required (section 11). - Sources: 1920×1080 is the commonest, then 1280×720; tall clips at 450×800 or 540×960 for phones and portrait tiles. Median source width 1,080px. - On the page: 16:9 41%, square 19%, portrait (4:5 to 9:16) 25%, 4:3 or 3:2 12%. Corners square on 75% (the rest 8px or less, or 20–32px). `object-fit: cover` on 84%, contain on 16% (product strips, letterboxed films). **Where it goes.** - **Hero background:** full-bleed, cover, often oversized by 1–25% so a drift or zoom never shows an edge. Either one slow take or a montage cutting every second or two. - **Inline, as a picture:** in splits, tiles and cards, at about a third of the width (median 33%, middle half 24–45%); a third of these clips are under a quarter of the width and fewer than one in ten is full width. Slow, near-still subjects (water, skin, light, a turning object) read as living photographs and sit well among stills. - **The frame that grows** (above), for a reel. - **A docked card** (above): one small clip in a corner. - **On hover:** only two or three sites play clips on hover, all of them in an index or list. Nothing that matters should play on hover only; phones have no hover. - **Full films:** about ten sites offer a full film behind a play button that opens a player with controls. None autoplays it. - **Sound:** six sites offer sound behind a toggle; no clip starts with sound. **How text sits on it.** - Of about 30 sites with a full-bleed picture or film behind text on the first screen, about 14 set the type straight on it and rely on the footage being graded dark where the type sits; about 10 dim it (to half brightness, under a 30–40% dark layer, or with a dark fade along the bottom 180–590px); about 6 keep the text off the picture, above it or on a solid card. - What goes on footage in the study is the name or a headline at 47–136px and one short line, docked bottom-left or centred. Where body text at 11–14px went on footage or a busy photograph, the panel named it as a fault, on top-scored sites too. - Here: one headline, one line and one action on footage at most, and never body text. Check contrast where the type sits across the whole loop, not only on the poster; if any frame drops below 4.5:1 (3:1 for type of 24px and up), use the scrim in section 6 or a solid band. **On the phone.** Footage re-crops to a full-screen portrait (a separate tall source, or `object-position` on the subject); inset frames go full-bleed. One site in the study adds a 40% scrim on the phone only, where the type covers more of the picture. ### Crops and treatment - **Ratios.** Of 1,356 pictures and clips measured: 4:5 21%, 16:9 19%, 1:1 16%, 16:10 10%, 3:2 7%, 2:3 5%, 4:3 5%, 5:4 4%, 3:4 3%, wider than 2:1 6%, 9:16 or taller 3%. Landscape 52%, portrait 33%, square 15%. - **Two ratios do most of the work.** On sites with four pictures or more, the two commonest ratios hold 76% of the pictures. The others (five ratios in all at the median) are exceptions with a reason: one tall portrait in a run of landscapes, one wide band. - **Square corners** on 94% of pictures; 62 of the 68 sites with pictures in the page keep at least 80% of them square. Where corners are rounded, it is 5px or less on two-thirds of them, or 20–32px on card interfaces, one value per site. - **Cover.** `object-fit: cover` on 78%, contain on 10% (a product on a tile, a letterboxed film). - **Untouched.** CSS filters touch pictures on only 9 sites, mostly for hover states. A handful use black-and-white photography as a set; two multiply scanned paper onto the ground. Several keep the interface black, white and grey and let the photographs carry all the colour. - **Common in the study, not treatments here** (section 6): a fixed grain layer over the whole page (about a third of the sites), duotone or tinted photographs, blurred copies behind a picture as a glow, tilted prints and stickers with offset shadows. - **Oversize only by the distance it moves.** 22 sites move pictures with the scroll, oversizing them by 1–25%. Oversize by the travel and no more, on one picture per screen. - **Resolution.** The study serves pictures at a median 1.9 times their CSS width, but 17% are served smaller than they are shown and full-width pictures at a median of only 1,440px. Here: twice the CSS width, capped at about 2,400px (section 4). ### Text over pictures - In the study, text sits on pictures often and is checked rarely: about 28 notes record text set straight on a picture with no scrim, and the faults of 16 sites include text lost over pictures: 8–14px labels and body over photographs, and navigation in a difference blend or with no backing passing over them. - Where it works, the text is display size and sits over the calm part (sky, a dark wall, the shadow side), docked in a corner or along one edge. Two other forms in the study: a solid card in the ground colour inset over the photograph and carrying the heading, and text on the white of a picture that fades into the page. - Here: on a picture put only display text, one short line and one action. Body text, captions and labels go beside or under it. Measure contrast at the text's own position (4.5:1, or 3:1 for 24px and up). If it fails, move the text to a calmer part, put it on a solid card in the ground colour, or use the scrim in section 6. A fixed navigation that passes over pictures gets a solid band, or hides while scrolling down. ### Rules for a generator 1. **About a third of the page is picture.** Across the scrolled screens, pictures fill 30–40% of the area, and at least one screen in four carries no picture (top sites: 30% and 28%). 2. **A picture leads its screen or stays small.** A leading picture takes at least 60% of its screen; an accent stays under 10% of it. Avoid screen after screen of pictures at 20–40%: in the study 42% of screens are 0% and 19% are 90% or more. 3. **Three to five placements per page,** and no two neighbouring sections with the same one. Sites with two or fewer average 7.31, sites with three or more about 7.5. 4. **Six to twelve pictures, never fewer than four.** Study median 7; top sites 4–27; lowest 2. 5. **Two ratios for at least 75% of the pictures** (76% in the study), a third only for a deliberate exception. Defaults: 4:5 for portraits, 16:9 or 3:2 for landscapes. 6. **Square corners on every picture** (94% in the study). If the direction rounds them, one radius of 4px for every picture and clip. 7. **Split pictures take 42–50% of the width, or two-thirds,** at the full height of the section and touching the viewport on their outer side; the text starts on the 50% line. On the phone the picture goes first, full width. 8. **Full-bleed bands are 100% wide and 100–150vh tall,** one every three or four screens, oversized by 10% at most for parallax, with text only in one corner at least 32px in. On the phone, re-crop to a full-screen portrait. 9. **One inset frame that grows per page,** from 35–50% of the width to the full screen over 720–2,700px of scroll, with nothing else moving on that screen. 10. **Horizontal galleries show three cards and a cut fourth:** cards 25–35% of the width with 16–20px gaps; on the phone one card at 75–80% of the width with the next one showing. 11. **One moving picture per screen.** Clips of 5–15s (median 10s), muted, looped, inline, with a poster, paused out of view; a hero source of 1920×1080 under 10MB, inline clips at 1280×720 or smaller under 5MB. 12. **Only display text on a picture:** a headline, one line and one action at most, with contrast measured at the text's position across the whole loop. Body text, 16px or more, goes beside or under the picture, never on it.

body:
# Inspecting Element Attributes

When the snapshot doesn't show an element's `id`, `class`, `data-*` attributes, or other DOM properties, use `eval` to inspect them.

## Examples

```bash
playwright-cli snapshot
# snapshot shows a button as e7 but doesn't reveal its id or data attributes

# get the element's id
playwright-cli eval "el => el.id" e7

# get all CSS classes
playwright-cli eval "el => el.className" e7

# get a specific attribute
playwright-cli eval "el => el.getAttribute('data-testid')" e7
playwright-cli eval "el => el.getAttribute('aria-label')" e7

# get a computed style property
playwright-cli eval "el => getComputedStyle(el).display" e7
```

body:
# Layout

How the page is put together: margins, the grid, where text sits, how sections differ, navigation,
endings and the phone. The direction sheet gives the specific compositions; this file gives the habits
behind them, taken from the panel's notes on the 114 studied sites that scored 7.3 or higher (counts
below are hand tallies from those notes, so read them as "about").

## Contents

1. What strong pages do
2. Margins and the grid
3. Where text sits
4. Empty space
5. The frame: margins, balance and titles
6. Sections: carry the idea, vary the arrangement
7. Navigation
8. Endings
9. The phone is a second composition
10. How pages fail

## 1. What strong pages do

- **Tight margins, content to the edges.** About 45 of 114 use outer margins of 32px or less; only
  about 8 use 80px or more. The centred 1100–1300px container is the minority among strong sites and
  the usual frame of the ones the panel called stock.
- **Text hangs from an off-centre line.** About 22 anchor text to one fixed line that is neither the
  centre nor the margin: a third across, 42%, the midpoint.
- **Two or three type sizes with nothing between** (about 30): one very large with one small, or
  everything small with the scale given to the image.
- **One thing per screen** (about 20): one statement, one object, one project.
- **Sections told apart by their ground.** About 20 change the whole background colour at each
  section; about 12 alternate light and dark; about 10 never change and separate by space alone.
- **Sections recomposed, not repeated.** About 14 rearrange every section; about 12 alternate a
  full-bleed image screen with a near-empty type screen.
- **The system broken once, on purpose** (about 14): one centred line on a split page, one paper card
  on a dark page, colour held back until the last screen.
- **Often no navigation bar** (about 45), and endings that are a designed scene rather than link
  columns.
- **Few words.** Median 575 on the whole study; some of the best carry under 200.

## 2. Margins and the grid

```css
:root {
  --margin: clamp(1rem, 2.2vw, 2rem);   /* 16–32px: tight, so content reaches the edges */
  --gutter: clamp(0.75rem, 1.4vw, 1.5rem);
}
.wrap { padding-inline: var(--margin); }
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(12, minmax(0, 1fr)); column-gap: var(--gutter); }
```

- One pair of margins and one grid for the whole page. Every left edge is a column line.
- Do not wrap the page in a `max-width: 1200px; margin: auto` container by reflex. Let large things
  (type, images, colour fields) run the full width, and constrain only the measure of running text
  (`max-width` in `ch` on the paragraph, not on the page).
- On very wide screens cap the layout at about 1760–1920px, or let type sized in `vw` stop growing with
  a `clamp()`.
- Directions that call for wide margins (uneven photographs, the quiet instrument) say so on the
  sheet; follow the sheet.
- Never draw the grid. Column lines, crosshairs and guides are banned ornaments here even though they
  are fashionable; the grid is felt through alignment.

## 3. Where text sits

- **Pick the anchor line and reuse it.** If the hero headline starts at column 5, the section
  headings, the pricing figure and the footer links start there too. Two or three anchor lines on a
  whole page; six means nothing was decided.
- **Off-centre beats centred.** A heading in the left third with its paragraph in the far-right
  column on the same baseline and nothing between; a headline in the bottom third under a deliberate
  void; text docked in corners with the middle given to the picture.
- **Opposite ends.** Two short texts at opposite ends of one baseline (name left, one-line description
  right) is the commonest alternative to the centred stack.
- **Centred is a decision.** When a strong page centres, it uses one axis with wide empty flanks and a
  single element per screen, not a centred stack of heading, paragraph and two buttons.
- **Rows for long copy:** heading in the left third, body in the right two-thirds, the same split for
  every row on the page.
- Stagger sparingly: a second line indented by a third so a two-line headline steps across the screen.

## 4. Empty space

Empty space is placed, not left over. In the study of 97 Sites of the Day captured in October 2026,
readers judged every large empty area either a rest, which something closes, or a hole, which nothing
closes. Strong sites have plenty of rests. About half of them still leave at least one hole, and the
holes are what visitors name ("big random blank spaces").

**A void is placed when something closes it.** In the readers' notes the closer is, most often:

- the picture itself (sky, ground, the object, the film) with the type docked at its edge;
- a picture across the void: the photograph at the far side of an empty band, the full-width row
  rising under a statement, the opposite picture in a stagger;
- the type: a headline large enough to span the space, or two short texts at the two ends of one
  baseline;
- on a one-screen page, the wordmark, the navigation and one fact in the corners, like a mount around
  a print.

About one closer in five in the study is a hairline or grid line. That device is banned here; close the
void with the picture, the type, a step in ground tone or a field of flat colour.

**Where holes come from.** In order of frequency in the study:

1. A gap between sections stretched too far: bands of 250–760px of plain ground.
2. Text in one half of a section and nothing in the other.
3. Content that arrives late: a reveal not yet fired, so the visitor scrolls onto bare ground while the
   words fade in.
4. A short block stretched to a full screen: a footer padded to the viewport height, a section title
   alone on a whole screen.
5. A pinned scene that holds almost nothing for several screens.
6. Pictures of different heights top-aligned in a row, leaving a hole under the short one.

**Rules**

- Decide where the void is and name what closes it. If nothing does, it is a hole: move the section's
  picture into it, make the main element bigger, or take the space out.
- Keep the void clean: no stray caption, no decorative shape, no faint watermark, no grid lines.
- Sections sit 120–240px apart on desktop, counted from the last line of one to the first line of the
  next (the median in the study is about 230–250px), and 72–112px on a phone. A change of ground
  colour lets the gap be a little smaller. More than about 40% of a screen of plain ground between two
  sections is a hole.
- The gap between sections is clearly larger than any gap inside one. Related things sit close and
  unrelated things far; a heading has at least twice as much space above it as below.
- No stretch of the page taller than about half a screen holds nothing at all. In the study, runs of a
  screen or more with nothing in the page were almost always scroll distance for a pinned scene; the
  pinned stage must then hold something at every scroll position.
- Content is in place on the first paint. An entrance moves what is already there (see `motion.md`);
  it never leaves a screen of bare ground while the words arrive.
- Size a section to its content. `min-height: 100vh` belongs to a section that fills the screen, not
  to a footer or a lone heading.
- In a row of pictures of different heights, align the bottoms or put something under the short one,
  or crop the row to one ratio.
- A rest is one thing on a screen: a single line, one object, one picture or a field of colour. Once
  per page at most. A screen of nothing is never a rest, and the inspector fails two near-empty screens.
- When a section looks empty, the answer is almost never "add something". Make the main element
  bigger, or cut the section.

## 5. The frame: margins, balance and titles

The frame is what readers judge before any detail: "no good margin", "everything is shifted to one
side", "no clear title", "random unclear sections". The inspector measures each of these. The numbers
are from the study of 97 Sites of the Day (October 2026).

**One pair of equal margins.**

- The left and right margins are the same, at every width. On the studied sites with scrolling
  sections the two sides match to a few pixels: 16 and 16, 20 and 21, 32 and 32, 140 and 137. No
  strong page in the study was pushed to one side.
- The usual margin is tight: median about 28px at 1440, half the sites between about 18 and 45px, a
  few at 80px or more. Here it is 16–32px (section 2), and never under 16px at any width, on the phone
  included. About one award site in seven sets text 8–15px from the edge; that studio habit is
  excluded here.
- The navigation sits on the same margins as the content. The commonest small fault in the study is a
  header on one inset and the page on another (40px against 20px, or 34px on the left against 10px on
  the right).
- A bleed is deliberate and starts from the margin: a row of pictures that runs off the right edge
  begins on the left margin; a display line that bleeds starts or ends on one. A bleed never moves the
  margin.
- Asymmetry belongs inside the frame: an off-centre anchor line (a third across, 42%, the centre line)
  on symmetric margins.

**Use the width the page has set up.**

- In the study about one text section in a hundred leaves half the width empty. Text that sits in one
  half is common, in roughly one site in three, but the other half then holds the section's own
  picture (most often), a full-bleed picture behind the text, a second column, a list or a figure.
- When the text takes one side, put the picture, the second column, the list or the large number on
  the other. Never leave the other half to plain ground.
- The middle counts too: a card at the left edge and a lone button at the right with the middle third
  empty is the same hole.
- The first screen counts too. When the sentence and the button take the left third above a name
  docked at the foot, the upper right holds something (the picture or film, one fact, the action) or
  the name grows up to meet them; in testing, 60% of a first screen left as plain ground under the
  navigation read as a hole, and the inspector now warns when one empty block takes 28% of the first
  screen or more.
- A display line fitted to the width is fitted by measurement (a small script that sets its size from
  the content box, or SVG text with `textLength`), never by a size guessed for one face: a name that
  starts on the margin and runs a few pixels off the other edge reads as a mistake.
- A centred composition has one axis, equal flanks and one thing on it, not a stack of heading,
  paragraph and two buttons.

**A title that says what this is, on the first screen.**

- Asked whether a stranger could say what the page is within five seconds, readers found that 40 of
  the 97 first screens say it in words, 42 say it only through pictures, small print or a bare name,
  and 15 do not say it at all. The last group lost usability and content points, not design points.
- Size alone does not do it: 66 of the 97 first screens carry a display-size line, but 26 of those are
  a name, a slogan or a place with nothing saying what is offered.
- The first screen has one `h1`, at display size (32px or more on desktop; on the clear first
  screens in the study mostly 50–150px), two lines at most, that says what this is: the name with
  what it does, the product with what it is for, the event with its date and place. If the `h1` is
  the name, the line under it, at 18px or more, says what the thing is.
- It is there on the first paint. About a third of the studied pages still showed a loader or nothing readable 4.5
  seconds.

**A heading on every section.**

- 82% of the text sections on the studied sites open with a heading: median 57px (40–96px for the
  middle half), about three and a half times the body size, one or two lines.
- Headings start on the outer margin or on the page's inner anchor line (in the study about a third
  each) and in the same place for every section. About a quarter of the headings in the study are
  centred; centre one moment per page here.
- Where a studied section has no heading, the usual stand-in is a small label: caps, mono or a number
  in brackets. All three are banned here. Put the label's words in a heading in the heading face at the
  section size ("The rooms", "How it works", "Prices"), set them on the anchor line, and let the first
  sentence carry the rest.
- A statement can open a section as its heading only when it names what the section holds.

## 6. Sections: carry the idea, vary the arrangement

The most common failure in every score band is a distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks:
icon cards, a three-up row, an accordion, a link-column footer. About 25 of the studied sites lose
points this way, including several above 7.5.

- **The idea survives to the last pixel.** Ask of each section, pricing and FAQ included: what does
  the page's idea do here? If the page is a menu, the prices are menu lines. If the name is a
  monument, the footer is the name again. If the object's shape is the motif, the button and the image
  masks carry it.
- **No two neighbours share a layout.** Use the shape of each dealt blueprint (list, split, statement,
  full-bleed, mosaic, table, strip, pinned …). Count them in the screenshot; a shape used three times
  is the template showing.
- **Alternate dense and empty, image and type, light and dark** so the scroll has rhythm.
- **A repeated module is for archives only** (a work index, a menu, a schedule). Anywhere else,
  repetition reads as a kit.
- **Break the system once.** After the page has established its rule, one planned exception (a single
  centred line, one inverted section, one image at a different scale) is what makes the rule visible.
- **Short pages are fine.** A quarter of the studied sites are one or two screens. Do not add sections
  to seem complete; each one must carry a claim (see `copy.md` §1).

## 7. Navigation

- The plain form: the wordmark at one end, three to five text links, one action, all at text size on
  the page ground with no bar, border or background. Median link count in the study is 3.
- It is also normal to have less: small links in the corners, a single action, or the navigation
  folded into the content (a list of section titles that is itself the index).
- If it stays fixed, it must never sit on top of content: check every scroll position in the
  screenshots, especially on the phone. Floating pill bars are where the panel most often recorded a
  nav covering text.
- On a phone: wordmark and one action in view; the links go in a simple full-screen sheet opened by a
  text button ("Menu"), or move to the footer when there are only three.
- Navigation is small furniture, however it is drawn. On desktop it takes no more than about a tenth
  of the first screen; on a phone it is one row. A blueprint that builds the navigation as a column of
  colour blocks or a stack of tabs gets that treatment on desktop only, and collapses to one row on
  the phone so the headline, the supporting sentence and the action stay in the first screen. In
  blind tests a nav that ate the hero cost a whole point of usability.

## 8. Endings

- The page should end on a designed scene. In the study: the name at full width (about 18 of 114), the
  hero repeated in inverted colours (about 12), a closing scene of its own such as the one contact
  fact set as a headline (about 14), or simply one quiet line (about 22). Link-column footers appear
  in the panel's notes only as criticism.
- The full-width name is strong but already a studio habit; use it when the direction is name-led,
  otherwise prefer the blueprint dealt for the footer.
- Put the practical facts (address, hours, email, legal line) in the text face at a readable size, on
  the same anchor lines as the rest of the page.

## 9. The phone is a second composition

Design the 390px screen as its own page, not the desktop page squeezed. Strong sites that neglect this
lose usability points; weak ones are often just broken.

- Each blueprint on the sheet has its own phone paragraph. Build it.
- Keep one dominant thing on the first screen. A wordmark that was 20vw wide on desktop might stack on
  two lines at 26vw on the phone and be even stronger.
- Re-author line breaks; re-crop images to portrait (`object-position` per breakpoint, or a different
  crop size in the image URL); keep unevenness with alternating widths rather than making everything
  full width.
- Margins 16–20px. Body text 16–18px. Touch targets at least 44px high.
- Check 390px in the inspector's screenshots for every round: sideways scroll and three-line headlines
  usually appear here first.

## 10. How pages fail

From the panel's notes on the 54 sites scoring under 6.8 (counts out of 54):

- The whole page is the category's stock template; swap the logo and it could be any competitor
  (about 20).
- Centred headline, pill badge, two buttons, screenshot or tile grid below (about 9).
- A distinctive hero, then stock modules in the usual order (about 8, and about 17 more in the middle
  band).
- A default typeface with no character (about 13).
- Text too small or too low in contrast (about 13); legibility lost over busy photographs (about 9).
- An undersized headline and no focal point (about 9).
- The page never says what the thing is, or shows no work (about 12 and 7).
- Thin content stretched over many screens, or a single gag (about 11).
- Gates, preloaders and entry pop-ups before any content (about 9).
- A phone layout that is the desktop shrunk, or broken (about 8).
- Fixed elements sitting on content; careless details such as colliding lines (about 7 and 5).

And the faults of the best sites, which are not to be copied: body text at 9–13px (about 24 of the 90
sites at 7.5 or more), information hidden behind the concept (about 20), the idea running out
mid-page (about 15), text over footage with no scrim (about 12), gates and blank first paints (about
12), floating elements colliding with content (about 11), and a first screen with no statement of what
this is and no action (about 9). Say what the thing is, and offer the action, on the first screen.

title: Motion
